## Causal chains from these memoranda

**C014-1** [months] (begins in Phase I) The task force's DRY SEASON campaign breaks the Can Giuoc security section from a notebook in December 1964 and the section's papers name a courier (EV012-2) → the courier's family is in the Special Branch census and the land register names the house he sleeps in, so G Squadron can watch the Rach Cat mooring the courier serves and Delta takes six of the Long An province committee with the finance ledgers on 14 March 1965 (EV014-2) → the ledgers name nineteen villages' collectors and the province's collections fall to about a third of the previous year's by December, which costs the Front the rice its piastres bought in a province where the titling had already ended rent (EV001-2) → the committee is rebuilt from the Rung Sat by August 1965 with region cadres, and it never again meets anywhere a boat can reach from a hamlet with a post, which is the first turn of the displacement that ends with the committees of the Delta living in Cambodia (EV014-5).

**C014-2** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase II) Delta's raids take 61 province and region committee members out of the Saigon belt and the upper Delta in 1966–67, on the task force's files (EV014-3) → COSVN issues the three-sentence rule in April 1967 and the committees of the upper Delta move to Memot, inside Cambodia, visiting their districts four or five nights every second month (EV014-5) → the Front's district administration in those provinces is run by courier at two months' remove, its collections fall to about a sixth of 1964's, and its senior cadre are therefore outside the reach of every allied instrument including this one, so that in 1969–71 the national file names men that nobody can touch (EV014-7, P4 end vector) → when Lon Nol's coup and the incursion of May 1970 push the Cambodian sanctuary north to Kratie, the Front's southern administration moves with it and is further from the Delta in 1971 than it has ever been, which is why the countryside of 1969–71 is the best the government has held and why none of it is a measure of the enemy's organisation being beaten.

**C014-3** [months] (begins in Phase II) Delta's teams go into the Laotian panhandle under the ambassador's limits from October 1965 and bring back 134 measured points, a third under canopy (EV014-4) → the coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut can put a GBU-31 on a truck park under trees for the first time, and does, through 1966–67 → Group 559's answer is the answer it gave to HARD CROSSING, which is to disperse what can be measured, so the parks fragment into a dozen dispersal sites each and the measured point loses its value within a season (POS005-4, F014-8) → the lasting product is not tonnage but the ledger: a team's count of what passed a junction on a given night is the only interdiction figure in this war that was never contested in Washington, and it is what makes the Commando Hunt claims of 1969–71 indefensible from the first week (EV000-55, EV000-68).

**C012-2**, written by memorandum 012 and terminating in an event this memorandum did not write, resolves differently now and in the enemy's favour. Its course was: STILL WATER drives the Hoc Mon committee out of its district → FOLLOW THROUGH reaches Cu Chi and takes the region finance section's ledger, and the committee and the section go to the Ho Bo woods → nobody quarters or guides the assault companies in the Ho Bo woods at Tet. With Delta raiding the base-area fringes from 1966, the Ho Bo woods is no longer far enough: the Hoc Mon committee and the region's finance section leave it for the Cambodian side of the Fishhook during 1967, as the Dinh Tuong committees left for Memot (EV014-5). The terminal link holds — nobody quarters the assault companies in January 1968 — and it holds harder, because the committee is now a border away rather than a day's walk. The cost is that the committee survives Tet intact where in memorandum 012's version it was within reach of a cross-province warrant. The chain's author predicted the outcome; he did not predict that a further provision would buy the same outcome at the price of putting the organisation permanently beyond arrest.

**C014-4** [months] (begins in Phase III) Delta's troops are used as urban assault infantry for nine days in Saigon and take 14 command posts, at a cost of nine dead and thirty-one wounded (EV014-6) → the unit is at about nine-tenths strength in its assault troops through the spring of 1968 and its raid rate in the Delta falls to about 25 a month, at the moment the Front's infrastructure in the Delta is most exposed by its own Tet losses → the senior cadre who would have been taken in that window are not taken, and the Front's provincial committees reconstitute from the base areas through the summer with cadres sent down from the region → by 1969 the file names a senior layer that is both intact and in Cambodia, and the best opportunity the provision ever had was spent clearing streets.

**C014-5** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase IV) Two men of G Squadron lie on a slope 1,400 metres from the camp at Son Tay for three nights in October 1970 and report empty cells, no cooking for prisoners and dry wells (EV000-69) → the Joint Chiefs cancel the raid on 2 November 1970, saving 116 aircraft, 56 raiders, an F-105G and about 42 PAVN guards → Hanoi never learns that its camps in the countryside can be reached, so the consolidation of the prisoners into the central prisons that followed the historical raid does not happen, and the men in the camps outside Hanoi stay dispersed through 1971 and 1972 under the regime they already had [H59] → the one American instrument that ever improved the prisoners' treatment was an operation that failed, and better intelligence removed it, so the prisoner issue reaches Paris in 1972–73 exactly as it did historically and the Republic's negotiating position gains nothing from the best reconnaissance capability in the war (F014-15, F014-23).

**C014-6** [months] (begins in Phase IV) Cooper–Church bars American ground troops and advisers from Laos and Cambodia on 29 December 1970 and MACV's lawyers read it as covering reconnaissance teams (EV014-11, EV000-70) → the last Delta teams come out of the panhandle on 19 January 1971 and the February programme into Base Areas 353 and 609 is cancelled → Lam Son 719 crosses into Laos on 8 February with the folders the teams built since 1965 and without the men who built them, against a 559th Group security system those men had watched for five years (EV000-71) → the one capability in this provision that nothing else in the war could replace turns out to have rested on an ambassador's discretion rather than on any authority, and it is removed by a sentence in an appropriations bill written about a different problem.

**C015-1** [months] (begins in Phase I, EV015-1) The Ghostriders answer the held belt's posts from January 1964 and Farm Gate's clearance takes half an hour → this headquarters and the Joint General Staff delegate clearance within 300 metres of a post to the district chief in July (F015-7) → the Front moves its assaults to the hamlet's edge, where a district chief whose post is under attack decides in minutes whether to fire on the hedge line (F015-5, F015-13) → the district chiefs of the merit list, chosen for their judgment, become the war's arbiters of civilian harm at night, and the Inspectorate's first cases against list chiefs in 1965 are for fire beside hamlets rather than for corruption [X-015].

**C015-2** [months] (begins in Phase II, EV008-4) The Dinh Tuong provincial unit draws the province's gunship to a diversion at Long Dinh and ambushes the relief at the culvert on 9 March 1967 → Liem's fourth rule puts a gunship over the road ahead of every night relief (EC015-2) → on 14 June the 514th's ambush is found in the cane and destroyed, and it never ambushes that road again on a clear night → the district's RF companies move by road at night again in the dry season of 1967–68, and the rule of fire first (POS008-4) relaxes in Cai Lay for the clear nights only, so that the district's posts have their reaction force back on the nights the gunship can see and only then [X-015].

**C015-3** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase I, EV015-2) The wing forbids attacks below 3,500 feet after Tam Quan in December 1964 → the coast's posts are attacked on monsoon nights through 1966, and eleven fall in Hoai Nhon and Phu My while a Ghostrider orbits above them (EV015-4) → Vinh Loc's figures send the VNAF's second gunship squadron to Nha Trang for the coast in 1967 rather than to Da Nang → from 1969 the coast of II Corps has the war's only all-weather night fire, and the 819th, not the 821st, is the squadron at Nha Trang that flies over Pleiku in 1975 (EV015-6, EV000-95) [X-015].

**C015-4** [months] (begins in Phase IV, EV015-7) The 817th flies Route 7 in support of the incursion and loses Spooky 34 to a 37mm battery near Snuol on 14 August 1970 → Khiem asks for the squadron's withdrawal to the Delta, where the posts need it and the guns are few → the squadron forms a five-aircraft detachment at Binh Thuy for the lower Delta (EV015-6) → at Xeo Mat in February 1971 the post's call is answered by a district gun and a Vietnamese gunship together, and Sergeant Danh Son adjusts both on one set (EV008-7) [X-015].

**C015-5** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase II, EV015-5) The gunship wing takes the VNAF's scarcest radar and avionics technicians from 1967 (F015-8, F015-10) → the Joint General Staff bars their transfer in 1971 to keep the wing flying (EV015-6) → in the ration of 1974 the JGS puts the wing's Binh Thuy detachment first on the fuel list because it is the one VNAF unit still fully manned, while a third of the VNAF is grounded → Military Region 9's rice campaign of the spring, planned on the reading that the VNAF is grounded, meets the gunships every night, and the harvest behind the canal posts goes to the government's buyers in Vi Thanh (EV015-8) [X-015].

## P014a · 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (SFOD-D, Delta Force), US Army, in its 2026 configuration and at full strength: the whole unit committed to Vietnam, with its assault squadrons, its reconnaissance and surveillance squadron, its organic aviation squadron and its support squadrons, without the wider JSOC package (no 160th SOAR, no dedicated JSOC ISR wing); missions: hunting PAVN and VC leadership and the infrastructure, COSVN and the base areas, POW recovery, raids into the North and reconnaissance, across the borders only where and when history's forces went
the whole unit, full commitment [U]; ~1,000–1,500 personnel of whom ~250–350 operators [E: open-source estimates of Delta's strength, D1] · spaces ~1,000–1,500 [E: the whole unit; no ceiling (CONFIG troop_ceiling = NONE)] · arrives 1964-09-01 · FIND, FIX, STRIKE, SUBVERT · ground

**Key figures.**
- Unit: established 19 November 1977 [M014·S1]; 2026 strength about 1,000–1,500, of whom about 250–350 operators [E: S1's 2001 figures grown by D Squadron and the support squadron]
- Organisation: four assault squadrons (two assault troops and a reconnaissance troop each; assault troop four teams of 5–6), G Squadron (advanced force), E Squadron (company of light helicopters and King Airs), signal and support squadrons [M014·S1] [M014·S2]
- Arrival 1 September 1964; headquarters 15 August 1964 [E: two weeks after the Tonkin reports]
- Borders as history: Laos from 18 October 1965 within the ambassador's limits; Cambodia from September 1967, foot reconnaissance only; the North only at Son Tay, 21 November 1970 [M014·S3] [M014·S5] [U]
- Raids in the South at maturity: about 40–120 a month; 15–35% reach a listed cadre at district level or above; about 80–400 such cadre a year [E: D5]
- Reconnaissance: 15–25 teams in the field at once, 40–80 team-missions a month [E: D5]; SOG's benchmark 454 Cambodian missions in 1969 [M014·S3]
- Replacement: about 30–50 operators a year from selection and the six-month OTC [E: S1]
- 2026 equipment stock about two to three years of wastage; thinning from 1966–68 [E: D8]
- History's benchmarks: JPRC never recovered an American POW (8 and 9 successes in 1968–69, 272 Vietnamese recovered) [M014·S6]; Son Tay empty, prisoners moved 14 July 1970 [M014·S5]; SOG's northern agents more than three-quarters captured [M014·S3]

**Negative specification.** Delta cannot find what no one has found. It finishes targets that the combined task force, the U-2S and Global Hawks, a defector or a captured document have located [M012] [M003]; it locates very little itself beyond the reach of its own patrols, and nothing under triple canopy from the air. It cannot destroy a main-force unit: a battalion of 400 is not a raid target for a troop of 20–24 operators [E: D2]. It cannot reach COSVN by raid while COSVN is in Cambodia, because no American ground force crosses that border until September 1967, and then only on reconnaissance on foot without air support, and with no exploitation force [M014·S3]; and COSVN, about 2,400 staff dispersed and mobile, evaded Junction City, Menu and the 1970 incursion [M014·S7]. It cannot raid the North before history's one raid at Son Tay in November 1970 [M014·S5]. It cannot enter Laos before October 1965 [M014·S3]. It brings no 160th SOAR and no drone orbit of its own [U]: its lift is a company of light helicopters [M014·S2], and any operation larger than a troop or deeper than their range needs the theater's lift. It cannot speak Vietnamese, so every target that comes through Vietnamese hands comes with the risk of a leak. It cannot be handed to the ARVN, and its 2026 equipment cannot be repaired in 1964 (D8). And it is not numerous: about 280–350 people who go on operations [E: D2], refilled at perhaps 30–50 a year.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy's senior cadre in the South the night. From 1964 a province committee member, a regional military commander or a COSVN courier who sleeps in a hamlet that the task force's files have named can be taken from his bed by men he cannot see, in 2–6 hours from the decision [E: D5]. It denies the infrastructure the comfort that only the hamlet cadre are hunted. It denies the base areas inside the South (the Iron Triangle, the Ho Bo woods, the Do Xa, the U Minh) their freedom from observation at night. It denies the Trail and the Cambodian base areas their freedom from observation from October 1965 and September 1967, within history's limits [M014·S3]. It denies Hanoi certainty that a prisoner camp in the South is beyond reach. It does not deny the enemy its main force, its sanctuaries or its strategy.

**Verdict.** Delta is the best night raid force in the world, put into a war fought at night by an enemy who believed the night was his. That is worth something real and specific: from late 1964 the senior infrastructure in the South (province committees, regional commanders, couriers and their documents) can be taken when it is found, at night, by men who see. The unit's whole value runs through the combined task force's files [M012]. Delta adds the hands for the hardest 10–20% of the task force's targets [E: D13] and the speed to reach them before they move. That will be 50–250 more senior cadre a year at maturity, against an infrastructure counted in the tens of thousands [E: D5]. It is reconnaissance that finds the Trail and the Cambodian base areas a little better than SOG did, from history's dates. It is a better POW recovery force than any history had. It does not touch the main force, the sanctuaries or Hanoi's decision. COSVN, which the provision names, is beyond its reach until 1970 and probably after, because it was a moving headquarters of 2,400 people in a country no American could enter [M014·S7]. The raid into the North that history made, the unit could make better. It is one raid. Delta is a scalpel. The war has places to use one, and it is not won with one.

## P014b · MACV Joint Special Operations Command (MACV-JSOC), newly formed after the Gulf of Tonkin incident: a joint headquarters under COMUSMACV that commands SFOD-D and the special operations units the user will assign to it later, with standing liaison to MACV J-2 and J-3, MACV-SOG, the CIA station, the Combined Interagency Task Force of memorandum 012, the Joint General Staff and the US Mission, for logistics, targeting and deconfliction
one headquarters, formed August 1964 [U]; ~250–450 personnel [E: D2] · spaces ~250–450 [E: a joint task force headquarters at the scale of the early JSOC of 1980–81; no ceiling (CONFIG)] · arrives 1964-08-15 · FIND, FIX, STRIKE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Formed 15 August 1964 [E: after the Tonkin reports of 2 and 4 August]; model JSOC, 15 December 1980 [M014·S8]; precedent MACV-SOG, 24 January 1964 [M014·S3]
- Strength about 250–450, of whom 40–80 in 15–20 liaison cells [E: D2]
- Liaison with MACV J-2 and J-3, SOG, the CIA station, the combined task force [M012], the air command, the four corps (US and ARVN), the JGS, the National Police, the US Mission and Vientiane [U] [E: judgment from the period's establishments and practice]
- Capacity: 2–6 operations at once, 40–150 a month; deconfliction 1–3 hours inside the South [E: D5]
- No cross-border authority; no authority over the CIA or the GVN [M014·S3] [U]
- Running cost about $10–20 million a year in 1964 prices, excluding Delta [E: judgment from the period's establishments and practice]

**Negative specification.** The headquarters cannot authorise any cross-border operation: Laos stays with the ambassador, Cambodia with Washington from September 1967, the North with the President [M014·S3] [M014·S5]. It holds no authority over the CIA, the GVN, the JGS or the National Police; it can only ask them. It brings no units except Delta, no aviation beyond Delta's own [M014·S2], no surveillance and no sources of its own: every target it acts on comes from someone else's files [M012] [M003]. It cannot stop leaks from Vietnamese channels it must use; it can only route around them. It is not a theater command, and it cannot direct the conventional war.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the seams between the American services, SOG, the CIA station and the combined task force, which a single raid force working through MACV J-3 would leave open: fewer raids planned through channels that leak, fewer sources burned, fewer teams shot by friendly fire.

**Verdict.** The headquarters is the price of using Delta well. Without it, Delta would work through MACV J-3 and the corps, its targets would pass through hands that leak, and its raids would collide with the task force's and SOG's. With it, a small joint staff keeps the targets in American hands, clears the ground for each raid in hours, and shares what the raids bring back. It adds nothing new to the war's knowledge. It adds speed and order to a scalpel. It is also the frame for the units the user will add later, and its value will grow or shrink with them.

# Card 015 — Gunship replacement: every US and RVNAF AC-47, AC-119 and AC-130 removed; 64 AC-130J Ghostrider to the USAF from 1964 and 48 AC-130U Spooky II to the VNAF from 1967

*Memorandum 015 · status complete · full record: memos/015/ · generated by fie.py*

## P015a · Lockheed Martin AC-130J Ghostrider gunship, Block 30 in its 2026 configuration (MC-130J airframe, Precision Strike Package: GAU-23/A 30mm chain gun, 105mm cannon, MX-20 and MX-25 electro-optical and infrared turrets with laser designators, wing stations for GBU-39/B Small Diameter Bombs and AGM-114 Hellfire, a ten-tube common launch tube for AGM-176 Griffin and GBU-69/B Small Glide Munition, AN/ALR-56M, AN/AAR-47 and AN/ALE-47 self-protection), replacing every USAF AC-47, AC-119 and AC-130 of the war, which with their programmes and infrastructure do not exist; missions suggested by the provision: close air support, armed overwatch and Trail interdiction
64 aircraft [U] · spaces ~1,900–2,400 in Southeast Asia, of whom ~1,100–1,500 in RVN [E: D2; about 1.5 crews of nine per aircraft and about 15–20 maintainers per aircraft, split between Phan Rang or Nha Trang and Ubon; no ceiling (CONFIG troop_ceiling = NONE)] · arrives 1964-01-01 · STRIKE, FIX, INTERDICT, SECURE · air

**Key figures.**
- 64 AC-130J Block 30 [U], 14th Air Commando Wing (Gunship), four squadrons of 16: Bien Hoa, Nha Trang, Da Nang, and Nha Trang then Ubon [E: D1]
- Crew 9 (two pilots, CSO, WSO, five SMAs) [M015·S4]; about 1,900–2,400 people in the wing, about 1,100–1,500 in RVN [E: D2]
- GAU-23/A 30mm and 105mm guns; up to eight GBU-39/Hellfire on the wings and ten Griffin or GBU-69 in the door [M015·S4]
- MX-20 and MX-25 EO/IR turrets with laser designators; no radar in the test reports — cannot aim its guns through cloud [M015·S4]
- 362 kt at 22,000 ft; ceiling 28,000 ft; range 3,000 miles [M015·S1] [M015·S2]; 4–6 hours on station at 150–250 nm [E: D5]
- Guns fired from about 7,000–12,000 ft above ground, against the AC-47's 1,500 ft [E: D5] [M015·S6]
- About 45–50 sorties a night sustained at 70–80% mission-capable [E: D10]
- Guided weapons production-limited: about 300–600 Griffin/GBU-69 a year [E: D8]
- History's peak gunship force was 53 aircraft of all types; 30 lost with about 160 crew [M015·S6] [M015·S7]

**Negative specification.** ### D14 · Negative specification

The Ghostrider cannot see through cloud. The Block 30 aircraft's operational test reports list no radar [M015·S4], and without one it cannot aim its guns through a monsoon overcast; under a 1,000–3,000-foot ceiling it either comes down into the guns or fires GPS weapons on coordinates the ground forces of this war cannot give it.

It cannot find a unit under triple canopy. It sees heat and light that leak through; a battalion in bivouac under the forest is invisible to it (A6).

It does nothing about the infrastructure. A gunship over a hamlet kills men who attack the hamlet; it cannot tell the tax collector from the farmer, and the VCI inside the hamlet are untouched by it (A6).

It does not stop the Trail. It kills trucks at night where it is allowed to fly and the guns are not; it does not reduce the tonnage arriving by more than the Trail's slack and repair allow, which is a few points (A7, POS005-4).

It is not survivable over SA-2 belts, and it is vulnerable on the ground. The wing's 64 aircraft are as exposed to a mortar at Bien Hoa as to a gun on the Trail.

It is not Vietnamese, and it cannot be made Vietnamese. It goes home with the Americans.

**Denies the enemy.** ### D15 · What it denies the enemy

It denies the enemy the night over a defended position. A VC or PAVN attack on an outpost, a district town or a fire base at night has been, in history, a contest the attacker could win before help arrived; with a Ghostrider over the post within 15–30 minutes, the attacker has the first hour, and after that the assault forming in the treeline is under 105mm fire it cannot hide from. It also denies him the open road at night in the panhandle, at a price in trucks, and the clear night in general. It does not deny him the cloudy night, the forest or the hamlet.

**Verdict.** ### D16 · Honest verdict

The Ghostrider is the best night close-support aircraft in the world, and it closes the gap the record has named for air power in this war: posts under attack at night (G-12). From the first night of 1964 the Republic's outposts, district towns and Special Forces camps can call down a gunship that arrives in minutes, sees the attackers in the dark at kilometres and kills them with a 105mm. That is a genuine transformation of one part of the war, and it comes three to four years earlier than history's gunships had any real numbers. It is not a transformation of the war. It does not see through monsoon cloud, it does not find the main force under the trees, it does not touch the infrastructure, and on the Trail it kills trucks the Trail can spare. Its value is that the enemy's best tactic of the village war, the night attack on an isolated post, becomes costly and often fails. Its limit is that the enemy chose that tactic because it was his best, and he has others.

**Pushes:** STRIKE.responsiveness -20 to -5 [minutes from a located target to fire on it (median, by the target type named in the note)] by the end of P2 (medium), RFPF.effectiveness.outpost_defence +2 to +7 [% of attacked outposts that hold] by the end of P2 (low), RFPF.effectiveness.reaction -1.5 to -0.3 [hours for relief to reach an attacked outpost] by the end of P2 (low), TRAIL.tonnage_arriving -10% to -3% of history's figure by the end of P4 (low), US.casualties -400 to -80 [US killed by hostile action in the calendar year in which the phase ends (Phase I: 1965)] by the end of P2 (low), AIR.losses -8 to +4 [US aircraft lost over the North and Laos in the phase] by the end of P4 (low), US.personnel_demand +1.1 to +1.5 [US military personnel in Vietnam, thousands] by the end of P2 (medium), POP.civilian_harm +0.2 to +1.5 [civilian dead and wounded in the South from all sides' operations, thousands a year] by the end of P2 (low), ENEMY.engagement_control -3 to 0 [% of engagements of platoon size or larger that the enemy initiates] by the end of P2 (low), POP.night_control.IV_corps 0 to +2 [% of IV Corps' rural population in hamlets the GVN holds after dark] by the end of P2 (low) · **Depends on:** POP.night_control, FIND.main_force, SANCT.laos, AIR.north_defences, LOG.distribution, ENEMY.engagement_control, TRAIL.capacity

## P015b · Lockheed/Boeing AC-130U Spooky II gunship (C-130H airframe; GAU-12/U 25mm Gatling gun, 40mm Bofors L/60 and 105mm M102 howitzer on trainable mounts, AN/APQ-180 synthetic-aperture strike radar, all-light-level television, infrared detection set, laser designators, dual-target fire control, armour and electronic countermeasures) in its final service configuration, to the Vietnamese Air Force from 1 January 1967, replacing every VNAF AC-47 and AC-119 of the war, which with their programmes and infrastructure do not exist
48 aircraft [U] · spaces ~250–450 US personnel in RVN, of whom ~150–300 military [E: D2; a training and advisory detachment and contractor field teams, falling after 1970; the crews and maintainers are VNAF; no ceiling (CONFIG)] · arrives 1967-01-01 · STRIKE, FIX, SECURE, ADVISE · air

**Key figures.**
- 48 AC-130U [U] to the VNAF from 1 January 1967 [U]: 81st Gunship Wing, 817th (Bien Hoa), 819th (Nha Trang), 821st (Da Nang) [E: D1]
- Crew 13 [M015·S3]; about 940 aircrew and 2,100–2,500 VNAF in the wing; 250–450 US advisers and contractors in 1967–69 [E: D2]
- GAU-12/U 25mm Gatling at 1,800 rpm, 40mm Bofors L/60, 105mm M102 [M015·S5]; no guided weapons
- AN/APQ-180 strike radar: fires through cloud [M015·S3] [M015·S5]; dual-target fire control on two targets 1 km apart [M015·S5]
- 300 mph; ceiling 25,000 ft; range about 1,300 nm; loiter 4.5 h; orbit 5,000–10,000 ft AGL [M015·S3] [M015·S5]
- First VNAF-crewed combat sortie about August 1967; all three squadrons at strength about end 1969 [E: D9]
- About 25–30 sorties a night at 50–60% mission-capable in 1968–72; 15–25 after 1973 [E: D10]
- 40mm and 105mm from in-theatre and domestic stocks; 25mm and radar spares only from the US aid line [E: D8]
- History's VNAF gunships: AC-47 from 1969, AC-119G/K from 1971–72, no radar [M015·S8] [M015·S9]

**Negative specification.** ### D14 · Negative specification

The U cannot find the main force under canopy, any more than any sensor can (A6). It cannot tell the cadre from the farmer, and it does nothing about the infrastructure.

It cannot survive radar-laid 37mm and 57mm, or the SA-2, and it is pressed above 10,000 feet by the SA-7 from 1972; against the PAVN's corps air defences of 1972 and 1975 it does not orbit over the battle.

It does not arrive as a capability in 1967. The aircraft arrive then; the crews and maintainers take until 1969 to reach strength, and the radar and fire-control technicians are the last.

It carries no guided weapons; its precision is its fire control and its radar.

It cannot be sustained by the RVNAF alone. Its radar and fire control need American contractors or depots, and its 25mm needs the aid line, for as long as it flies.

It is not a substitute for American air power in a conventional offensive. Three squadrons of gunships do not break a siege of the kind An Loc and Kontum were.

**Denies the enemy.** ### D15 · What it denies the enemy

It denies the enemy the night attack on a post after the Americans leave. History's VNAF had no answer to the PAVN's and the VC's night attacks on RF and PF outposts in 1973–74, and the land-grabbing war of those years ran on them; a Vietnamese gunship with a radar takes the monsoon night away from that war. It denies him nothing in the forest, nothing in the hamlet's politics, and little in a set-piece offensive with corps air defences.

**Verdict.** ### D16 · Honest verdict

The Spooky II is the most important aircraft the Vietnamese Air Force has ever been given, and it will take three years to be worth what it is. Once its crews and technicians are trained, it gives the Republic something history's never had: its own night and all-weather fire over its own outposts, from a crew that speaks the language of the man calling for it. That matters most after 1973, when every American aircraft has gone and the war in the countryside is a war of outposts attacked at night. It does not change the war's set-piece battles; it cannot survive the PAVN's corps air defences, it does not break a siege, and it lives on the appropriation for its radar, its 25mm and its contractors. Its value is that it makes the territorial war of 1973–74 one the Republic can fight on its own at night, and makes the outposts that fell in history to a night attack, many of them, hold. That is not a rung of the ladder. It is a part of the self-sufficiency the next rung needs.

## Trajectory Log

## Memo 014 — 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (Delta Force) at full commitment, under a newly formed MACV joint special operations command from August 1964

Memorandum 014 put the best raid force in the world into a war fought at night, and the war answered it with a circular. From September 1964 Delta and a new joint headquarters at Tan Son Nhut gave the attack on the Front's political apparatus a finishing arm for the targets the police and the task force could not reach: 297 cadre at district level or above in 1966–67, 61 of them province or region committee members, taken alive with their ledgers, four raids in five of them in III and IV Corps where the file was thick. In April 1967 COSVN told its senior cadre to stop sleeping in hamlets and to meet across the border, and by that autumn twenty-three raids in the best-filed province in the Delta found two men and twenty-one empty beds. The apparatus was driven out of the provinces it ran and permanently beyond arrest. Delta also brought this war its first coordinates from under the canopy, cancelled the Son Tay raid by reconnoitring it, and left in 1973 with everything that made it work. The end state is unchanged at rung (b).

## Memo 015 — Gunship replacement: every US and RVNAF AC-47, AC-119 and AC-130 removed; 64 AC-130J Ghostrider to the USAF from 1964 and 48 AC-130U Spooky II to the VNAF from 1967

Memorandum 015 replaced every gunship of the war with sixty-four AC-130J Ghostriders from the first night of 1964 and gave the Vietnamese Air Force forty-eight radar-carrying AC-130U Spooky IIs from 1967. It answered the question fourteen memoranda had left open: the post could call, and now something came in the dark. The Front stopped assaulting covered posts on clear nights within months and moved its war into the monsoon cloud, beyond the net and into the hamlets, where the coast's posts fell under a blind gunship in 1966. On the Trail the gunships killed three or four times history's trucks and the tonnage barely noticed. The lasting change was Vietnamese. From 1969 the VNAF's radar gunships held the posts' nights through cloud and in their own language, and they stayed: in the spring of 1974 they beat Military Region 9's rice campaign in Chuong Thien. They could not fly over the PAVN's divisions, and Thuong Duc and Pleiku went as before. The end state stays at rung (b), with the Republic's fall expected in 1976.
